name: cuba
why: Real multidimensional numerical integration from particle physics, a genuine research tool you could run at home.

brief.what_it_is: Cuba is a C/C++, Fortran, and Mathematica library for multidimensional numerical integration. You give it an integrand function and integration bounds, and it returns the integral's value along with an error estimate and a χ²-probability that indicates how reliable that error estimate is. It offers four interchangeable routines (Vegas, Suave, Divonne, and Cuhre) with nearly identical calling conventions, so you can swap one for another to cross-check results. It can also integrate vector-valued integrands and parallelizes the sampling automatically in Fortran and C/C++.
brief.why_it_exists: The page frames it as a tool for numerical integration in particle physics: different methods suit different integrands, so a researcher needs several routines with a common interface to compare results and to reach high precision when needed. The page describes the library as developed at the Max Planck Institute for Physics in Munich by Thomas Hahn.
brief.how_it_works: Vegas, Suave, and Divonne are Monte Carlo or stratified-sampling methods that draw quasi-random (Sobol or Korobov) or pseudo-random (Mersenne Twister or Ranlux) points, using importance sampling, globally adaptive subdivision, or numerical-optimization-guided partitioning. Cuhre is deterministic: it uses a cubature rule on subregions and, in each iteration, halves the subregion with the largest error along the axis with the largest fourth difference. The page notes that Cuhre is usually the only practical choice for relative accuracies much below 1e–3.

brief.install_notes: Source is distributed as a tarball (latest Cuba-4.2.2.tar.gz, about 744 kB); the page says the source compiles with gcc. The C functions can be called from Fortran directly without adapter code. Prebuilt Mathematica MathLink executables (version 4.2) are offered for Linux x86-64, macOS x86-64, and Cygwin/Windows, each as a gzipped file that needs gunzip and chmod 755. Windows native builds are not supported: Cuba 3 and later use fork(2), so Windows users are pointed to Cygwin. Third-party wrappers exist for Maple, REDUCE, R, Python, Julia, and Rust. The page does not give a Homebrew-specific procedure.
brief.standout: Four quite different algorithms share one calling interface, so cross-checking one integral against another is a matter of changing a routine name. The page also flags that most questions concern bounds other than the unit hypercube, and answers it by scaling the integrand with a Jacobian rather than changing the bounds, which it shows in a Fortran snippet.
brief.status: Quiet. The homepage lists Cuba-4.2.2.tar.gz as the latest release, dated 28 Feb 2022, with a fix for a potential segfault in divonne/Split.c, and the page says 'Last update: 28 Feb 22'. The page lists no newer release. I did not check a code repository for later commits, so the status is inferred from the homepage only.
brief.caveats: Windows is not supported natively; it needs Cygwin because of the fork(2) dependency. Prebuilt executables exist only for x86-64 Linux, x86-64 macOS, and Cygwin/Windows. Licensing is the GNU Lesser General Public License, and the page advises checking its terms before commercial use. Vegas is described as only sometimes competitive in sample count. Divonne is a development of the CERNLIB routine D151. The homepage is an academic site with plain HTML, and the page does not mention a changelog beyond the 4.2.2 note.
quotes: The Cuba library offers a choice of four independent routines for multidimensional numerical integration: Vegas, Suave, Divonne, and Cuhre.
Cuhre is quite powerful in moderate dimensions, and is usually the only viable method to obtain high precision, say relative accuracies much below 1e–3.

Upward of 75% of all questions regarding Cuba have to do with how to choose bounds different from the unit hypercube in Fortran, C, and C++. The solution is not to choose bounds but to scale the integrand.
